procedural_history.originating_court: Urban Estate Hisar Police Station, District Hisar (where FIR No. 95 of 2021 was lodged)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order passed by the High Court of Punjab & Haryana dated 05.04.2022 in Criminal Main No. 14198-2022 (CRM-M-14198-2022)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant (sole accused) filed a quashing petition (CRM-M-14198-2022) before the High Court of Punjab & Haryana seeking to quash the chargesheet dated 13.10.2021 for offences under Sections 323, 406, 498A, and 506 of the IPC. The High Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings, rejecting the petition in its order dated 05.04.2022.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's refusal to quash the criminal proceedings, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court heard the learned counsel for the petitioner and allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court.

decision.conviction_status: The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is hereby set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in declining to exercise its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to quash criminal proceedings arising from a matrimonial dispute, particularly when the allegations are general and sweeping.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed by a wife against her husband (the appellant) under sections 323, 406, 498A, and 506 of the IPC, alleging dowry demands and mental/physical trauma.
After investigation, the police filed a chargesheet only against the husband.
The husband filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) to quash the criminal proceedings.
The High Court declined to quash the proceedings, stating that the truthfulness of the allegations should be decided at trial.
The husband appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., the High Court has inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice.

In cases arising from matrimonial disputes, the court has a duty to thoroughly scrutinize the allegations to determine if there is any truth to them or if they are made solely to involve individuals in a criminal case.
Forcing a person to face a criminal trial based on general and sweeping allegations, without specific instances of criminal conduct, is an abuse of the process of the court.
application: The Supreme Court found that the allegations against the husband were general and sweeping in nature.
It reasoned that the High Court failed in its duty to subject these allegations to a thorough scrutiny, especially given the context of a matrimonial dispute.
The Court determined that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue based on such vague allegations would be an abuse of the process of law and a travesty of justice.
The Court also noted that the FIR was filed after a significant delay and only after the husband had filed for divorce, suggesting it was intended to harass the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in declining to exercise its inherent power. It held that this was a fit case for the High Court to have quashed the criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. because they were founded on general and sweeping allegations and their continuation would amount to an abuse of the legal process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in declining to exercise its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to quash criminal proceedings arising from a matrimonial dispute, particularly when the allegations are general and sweeping.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, implied by the issue and the appeal's success, is that the High Court was not justified in refusing to quash the criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., as the allegations were general and sweeping in nature.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in not inquiring into the truthfulness or reliability of the allegations, as that is the role of the trial court.
Once allegations disclose the commission of a cognizable offense, the question of whether they are true or false should be left for the trial court to decide based on evidence.
The police conducted a fair investigation and found sufficient reason to file a chargesheet against the appellant, while dropping proceedings against four other accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. must be exercised sparingly, carefully, and with caution. This power does not confer new authority but saves the court's pre-existing inherent power. It can be exercised only under three circumstances: (i) to give effect to an order under the Code, (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of the Court, and (iii) to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
obiter: A serious relook of the entire provision is warranted by the legislation, as it is common knowledge that exaggerated versions of incidents and a tendency for over-implication are reflected in a large number of complaints.
The courts would not encourage such disputes.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The authority of the court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure exists for the advancement of justice and to prevent its abuse. It would be an abuse of the process of the court to allow any action which would result in injustice. Therefore, a court is justified in quashing any proceeding if it finds that its initiation or continuance amounts to an abuse of the process of court or if quashing the proceedings would otherwise serve the ends of justice. When a complaint is sought to be quashed, it is permissible for the court to look into the materials to assess what the complainant has alleged and whether any offence is made out, even if the allegations are accepted in toto.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent power under Section 482 is to be exercised ex debito justitiae to do real and substantial justice for the administration of which alone courts exist.

The court can quash proceedings if it finds that the initiation or continuance of it amounts to abuse of the process of court or quashing of these proceedings would otherwise serve the ends of justice.

When a complaint is sought to be quashed, it is permissible to look into the materials to assess what the complainant has alleged and whether any offence is made out even if the allegations are accepted in toto.
policy_considerations: The ultimate object of justice is to find out the truth and punish the guilty and protect the innocent.
The tendency of implicating husband and all his immediate [relatives]... To find out the truth is a herculean task in majority of these complaints.
There is a need to maintain a balance between individual liberty and societal order while exercising the power of arrest.

No arrest can be made in a routine manner on a mere allegation of commission of an offence made against a person. It would be prudent and wise for a police officer that no arrest is made without a reasonable satisfaction reached after some investigation as to the genuineness of the allegation.
